title: Ionic, Covalent and Metallic Bonding
description: Three ways atoms join, and the properties each kind of bond gives.
hero_image_caption: Every solid material owes its character to the invisible architecture of its bonds — transfer, share or delocalise.
content_html:
Why Atoms Bond

Atoms bond together because doing so lowers their energy and gives each atom a full outer electron shell — the same stable arrangement as a noble gas. There are three main types of chemical bond, each arising from a different way of achieving this stability: ionic bonding, covalent bonding, and metallic bonding. The type of bonding determines a substance's properties — its melting point, conductivity, and physical strength.

Key Fact

Ionic: metal + non-metal, electrons transferred. Covalent: non-metal + non-metal, electrons shared. Metallic: metal atoms, electrons delocalised. Bond type determines properties — knowing which type applies is the first step in any bonding question.

Ionic Bonding

When a metal reacts with a non-metal, electrons are transferred from the metal atom to the non-metal atom. The metal loses one or more electrons to form a cation (positive ion), while the non-metal gains electrons to form an anion (negative ion). Both ions now have full outer shells and are stable.

The strong electrostatic attraction between the oppositely charged ions is the ionic bond. In sodium chloride (NaCl), for example, sodium loses one electron to become \(Na^+\) and chlorine gains one electron to become \(Cl^-\). These ions pack together in a regular three-dimensional arrangement called a giant ionic lattice.

In a dot-and-cross diagram for ionic bonding, draw the outer-shell electrons of each atom (dots for one, crosses for the other). Show an arrow from the metal to the non-metal indicating the electron being transferred, then draw the resulting ions with square brackets and the charge written outside. Only outer-shell electrons are shown — inner shells are omitted for clarity.

For magnesium oxide (MgO): magnesium (2,8,2) loses 2 electrons to become \(Mg^{2+}\), and oxygen (2,6) gains 2 electrons to become \(O^{2-}\). Both now have an outer shell of 8.

Properties from Ionic Bonding

Giant ionic lattices have characteristic properties. Their melting and boiling points are high because large amounts of energy are needed to overcome the strong electrostatic forces acting in all directions. When an ionic compound is solid, the ions are fixed in position — it does not conduct electricity. When melted or dissolved in water, the ions are free to move and carry charge, so the compound does conduct electricity.

Key Fact

Ionic compounds: high melting points (strong forces in all directions), brittle (layers of ions shift so like charges repel), conduct when molten or dissolved (ions move freely), but not when solid (ions fixed in lattice).

Covalent Bonding

Non-metals bond with other non-metals by sharing pairs of electrons. Each shared pair counts as one covalent bond. Both atoms contribute one electron to each shared pair, and by sharing, both achieve a full outer shell. Examples of simple covalent molecules include:

  • \(H_2\) — a single covalent bond (one shared pair)
  • \(O_2\) — a double covalent bond (two shared pairs: \(O=O\))
  • \(N_2\) — a triple covalent bond (three shared pairs: \(N \equiv N\))
  • \(H_2O\) — two single bonds; \(CO_2\) — two double bonds (\(O=C=O\))

Simple covalent molecules have strong bonds within each molecule but only weak intermolecular forces between molecules. This is why many simple covalent substances are gases or liquids at room temperature — it takes very little energy to separate the molecules from each other.

A student is given two white solids — sodium chloride (NaCl) and glucose (\(C_6H_{12}O_6\)) — and asked to identify which is which using only a conductivity test on dissolved samples and a melting-point check.

Step 1: Predict the bonding. NaCl is metal + non-metal → ionic. Glucose is non-metal only → covalent.

Step 2: Predict the properties. NaCl solution conducts electricity (free ions). Glucose solution does not conduct (no ions). NaCl has a very high melting point; glucose melts at a much lower temperature.

Step 3: Carry out the tests and match observations to predictions. The solid that conducts in solution and resists melting is NaCl.

Metallic Bonding

In metals, the outer electrons leave their atoms and form a sea of delocalised electrons. The metal is then a lattice of positive ions surrounded by this mobile electron sea. The metallic bond is the strong electrostatic attraction between these positive ions and the delocalised electrons.

This structure directly explains the key properties of metals. The delocalised electrons carry charge easily, so metals are excellent electrical conductors. They also transfer thermal energy readily, making them good thermal conductors. When a force is applied, layers of ions can slide over each other without breaking the bond — the electron sea simply flows around them — so metals are malleable (can be hammered into shape) and ductile (can be drawn into wires).

Key Fact

Metallic bonding: positive metal ions in a sea of delocalised electrons. This explains conductivity (mobile electrons carry charge), malleability (layers slide without breaking), and high melting point (strong attraction throughout the lattice).

A very common error is to say that aluminium rusts. It does not. Rust is specifically iron(III) oxide formed on iron or steel. Aluminium does react with oxygen in the air, but it instantly forms a thin, hard layer of aluminium oxide (\(Al_2O_3\)) on its surface. This oxide layer is tightly bonded to the metal beneath and acts as a protective barrier, preventing further oxidation. This is why aluminium products — bike frames, aircraft fuselage panels, drinks cans — appear unchanged after years of exposure to air and moisture.

Iron's oxide (rust) is flaky and porous, allowing oxygen and water to continue reaching the metal underneath. Aluminium's oxide layer is self-sealing — once formed, it stops further attack. This is a key difference for any compare-or-contrast question on metal properties.
exam_tip_html: For 4-mark compare-or-contrast questions on bonding, always give a named example for each bond type and link the bond to at least one property. For the 6-mark extended-response question on metallic bonding, structure your answer around the sea of delocalised electrons — explain what it is, then use it to account for conductivity, malleability and high melting point separately. Avoid saying aluminium 'rusts' — this is a common error flagged in examiner reports.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Ionic bonding: metal transfers electrons to non-metal, forming cations and anions held in a giant ionic lattice. High melting point; conducts when molten or dissolved.
  • Covalent bonding: non-metals share electron pairs. Simple molecules have low melting points (weak intermolecular forces); giant covalent structures have very high melting points.
  • Metallic bonding: positive ions in a sea of delocalised electrons. Explains electrical and thermal conductivity, malleability and ductility. Aluminium does not rust — its oxide layer protects it.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes ionic bonding?
A) Sharing of electrons between two non-metal atoms
B) Transfer of electrons from a metal atom to a non-metal atom
C) Delocalised electrons moving freely between metal ions
D) Attraction between molecules caused by weak intermolecular forces
practice_questions.marks: B) Transfer of electrons from a metal atom to a non-metal atom [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by a 'delocalised electron' in a metal.
practice_questions.marks: An electron that has left its parent atom [1] and is free to move throughout the metal structure / is not associated with any particular atom [1].

practice_questions.text: Describe how a dot-and-cross diagram shows the formation of magnesium oxide (MgO) by ionic bonding.
practice_questions.marks: Draw outer-shell electrons of Mg (2) and O (6) [1]; show transfer of 2 electrons from Mg to O [1]; draw resulting ions with charges Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ in square brackets with a full outer shell of 8 electrons on oxygen [1].

practice_questions.text:
Explain why sodium chloride has a high melting point but does not conduct electricity when solid, yet conducts when dissolved in water.
Use your knowledge of ionic bonding in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: High melting point: strong electrostatic forces between oppositely charged ions in all directions [1] require a large amount of energy to overcome [1]. Does not conduct when solid: ions are fixed in the lattice and cannot move [1]. Conducts when dissolved: ions are free to move and carry charge through the solution [1].

practice_questions.text: A student states that 'aluminium rusts in air, just like iron.' Explain why this statement is incorrect, and describe what actually happens to aluminium when it is exposed to air.
practice_questions.marks: StudyVault Mastering: identifies that rust is specifically an iron compound (iron(III) oxide) [1]; explains aluminium reacts with oxygen but forms a thin oxide layer (Al₂O₃) [1]; this layer is tightly bonded and impermeable, preventing further oxidation [1]; contrasts with iron's flaky, porous rust layer that allows continued attack [1]; concludes that aluminium appears unreactive in air because of this self-sealing protection [1]. Secure: first three points. Developing: two points with partial explanation.

practice_questions.text: Compare ionic bonding and metallic bonding in terms of the particles involved, the nature of the attractive force, and the electrical conductivity of each type of substance.
practice_questions.marks: StudyVault Mastering: Ionic — metal cations and non-metal anions [1], held by electrostatic attraction between opposite charges in a giant lattice [1], conducts only when molten or dissolved (ions free to move) [1]. Metallic — positive metal ions and a sea of delocalised electrons [1], held by electrostatic attraction between ions and electron sea [1], conducts in all states because delocalised electrons are always free to move [1]. Secure: four points with correct reasoning. Developing: three points.

knowledge_checks.q: In ionic bonding, which particles are transferred?
Which type of bonding involves a 'sea of delocalised electrons'?
Why does sodium chloride conduct electricity when dissolved in water but not when solid: _____
options: It gains extra electrons when dissolved
Its ions are fixed in place when solid but free to move in solution
Water adds ions to the compound
knowledge_checks.explanation: The correct answer is Its ions are fixed in place when solid but free to move in solution.

knowledge_checks.q: Aluminium appears to be unreactive in air because it ___.: _____
options: Does not react with oxygen at all
Forms a protective oxide layer that prevents further reaction
knowledge_checks.explanation: The correct answer is Forms a protective oxide layer that prevents further reaction.

knowledge_checks.explanation: Review the key terms and definitions covered in this lesson.

flashcard_questions.a: The strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions formed when electrons are transferred from a metal atom to a non-metal atom.
A bond formed when two non-metal atoms share a pair of electrons, giving both atoms a full outer shell.
The strong electrostatic attraction between a lattice of positive metal ions and the surrounding sea of delocalised electrons.

flashcard_questions.q: Why are metals good electrical conductors?
flashcard_questions.a: Their delocalised electrons are free to move throughout the structure, carrying charge easily.
Layers of positive ions can slide over each other without breaking the bond, because the electron sea flows around them.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a giant ionic lattice?
flashcard_questions.a: A regular, repeating three-dimensional arrangement of positive and negative ions held together by strong electrostatic forces acting in all directions.

flashcard_questions.q: What does Does aluminium rust? Explain state?
flashcard_questions.a: No. Rust is specific to iron. Aluminium forms a thin, tightly bonded oxide layer that acts as a self-sealing barrier, preventing further oxidation.

flashcard_questions.q: Why do simple molecular substances have low melting points?
flashcard_questions.a: The covalent bonds within each molecule are strong, but the intermolecular forces between molecules are weak and require little energy to overcome.

glossary_terms.definition: The strong electrostatic force of attraction between oppositely charged ions, formed when a metal atom transfers electrons to a non-metal atom.
A bond formed when two non-metal atoms share one or more pairs of electrons, giving both atoms a full outer shell.
The strong electrostatic attraction between a lattice of positive metal ions and the surrounding sea of delocalised electrons.
A regular, repeating three-dimensional arrangement of positive and negative ions held together by strong electrostatic forces acting in all directions.
Electrons that have left their parent atoms and are free to move throughout the metal structure, enabling electrical conduction and metallic bonding.
A positively charged ion formed when an atom loses electrons. Metal atoms form cations in ionic bonding.
A negatively charged ion formed when an atom gains electrons. Non-metal atoms form anions in ionic bonding.
Weak attractive forces between separate molecules. Much weaker than covalent bonds, they are responsible for the low melting points of simple molecular substances.
A diagram showing only the outer-shell electrons of each atom, using dots for one atom and crosses for another, to illustrate electron transfer or sharing in bonding.
